title: What is Apache Flink: another engine for processing data, but designed specially for real-time streaming (processes each event as it arrives, not in batches like Spark's default mode).
keyPoints: Flink is an open-source distributed stream-processing engine that processes each event as it arrives with sub-second latency.
It distinguishes event time from processing time and uses watermarks to handle out-of-order and late data correctly.
Keyed state is first-class and backed by configurable state backends such as HashMapStateBackend or RocksDB for large state.
Distributed checkpointing with lightweight barriers gives exactly-once state consistency and, with transactional sinks, end-to-end exactly-once.
Flink treats batch as a special case of streaming over a bounded dataset so one API serves both.
The DataStream API gives low-level control while the Table API and Flink SQL provide declarative relational queries with optimizer support.
Flink is the engine of choice for real-time fraud scoring, live risk limits, and instant settlement signals where correctness and latency both matter.

s1_definition.oneliner: Apache Flink is a distributed stream-processing engine that processes each event as it arrives with event-time semantics, keyed state, and exactly-once guarantees.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Stream-first engine** – Flink treats a stream as the fundamental primitive and processes each record the instant it arrives, unlike micro-batch systems that group events into small batches.
- **Event-time processing** – It distinguishes event time (when it happened) from processing time (when the engine sees it) and uses watermarks to handle out-of-order data.
- **Stateful processing** – Keyed state is first-class, backed by configurable state backends such as HashMapStateBackend for fast in-memory access or RocksDBStateBackend for large state that exceeds heap.
- **Exactly-once guarantees** – Distributed checkpointing with lightweight barriers snapshots all operator state and source offsets, giving exactly-once state consistency and, with transactional sinks, end-to-end exactly-once.
- **Unified batch and streaming** – Flink treats batch as a special, bounded case of streaming so the same API serves both use cases.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's fraud desk. Spark's default mode is like a supervisor who collects card swipes into small stacks and checks each stack every few seconds. Flink is like a sharp officer who inspects every single swipe the instant it lands on the counter, remembers each customer's recent pattern in a personal ledger (state), and can tell that Priya's card was used in two cities one minute apart right now, not a few seconds late. Flink also keeps a reliable notebook (checkpoint) so if the officer faints, a replacement resumes from the exact last page with no swipe double-counted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Flink is an open-source distributed stream-processing engine built for true record-at-a-time processing with very low latency and strong correctness guarantees. Its signature difference from a micro-batch system like Spark Structured Streaming is that Flink treats a stream as the fundamental primitive and processes each event the instant it arrives, rather than grouping events into small batches, so latency can be in the low milliseconds. Flink even treats batch as a special case of streaming over a bounded dataset, so one API serves both.

Flink's standout features are time handling, state, and correctness. For time, it distinguishes event time from processing time and uses watermarks to decide when a window is complete, with configurable allowed lateness for stragglers. For state, keyed state is first-class: each key, such as a bank account, can keep running state like a count or last-seen location, managed in a state backend that can be in-memory or RocksDB for very large state, which makes stateful fraud rules natural and scalable. For correctness, Flink takes periodic distributed checkpoints of all operator state and source offsets using lightweight barriers, so after a failure it restores the latest checkpoint and replays from saved offsets, giving exactly-once state semantics, and with transactional sinks that extends to exactly-once end to end.

At the National Bank of India this was the engine we reached for whenever real time and correctness both mattered, like real-time fraud scoring. The job keyed the swipe stream by account, kept a per-account count inside a one-minute event-time window, and fired an alert the instant an account exceeded its allowed swipes. Because state was checkpointed, even a mid-stream crash and restore did not lose the running counts or double-count a swipe. The DataStream API gave us full control for the custom fraud rules, while the Table API and Flink SQL served the reporting aggregations that analysts maintained.

That combination of event-at-a-time latency, rich keyed state, event-time windows, and exactly-once guarantees is exactly why a bank chooses Flink for its most demanding streaming workloads.

Remember one sentence: Flink is a true event-at-a-time streaming engine with event-time watermarks, keyed state, and exactly-once checkpointing that processes each record the instant it arrives.
